Mr. Fortune gives curious description of Chi

ern Chinese things, all well known in England
such, for example, as cymbidium chinense, olea
fragrans, oranges, roses, camelias magnolias etc.
and, of course, multitude of dwarf trees without
which no Chinese garden would be considered com
plete. In the alcOve alluded to there are some

that of southern China. The floor of this BUILDING

the visitor gets good view of the water and other
objects of interest in the garden That this is a
fav0rite lounge and smoking place with the Chi
nese, the following Chinese notice, which we found
on one of the pillars, will testify: "A Careful and
Earnest Notce-This garden earnestly requests that

ors; great deal has been expendedin planting and

a still, sultry afternoon. The woods
and meadows, the thousand towers of
the city, were bathed in bright sun-
shine; but beyond the latter lowered,
black as ink, pile of thunder clouds.
The threatening background rose, let-
ting fall a shifting curtain of dark
gray, from the feet of which whirled
clouds of tawny dust, veiling the
splendor of the distant domes. As
the storm advanced, columns of dust
arose, here and there, all over the
city shadow, as of night, crept
across it, leaving only the nearer
spires to blaze with double splendor
against the black chaos. Presently
the more distant portions of the city
were blotted out. The brighter tow-
ers remained for time visible, shi-
ming specially through the falling
cloud, and seeming to be removed far
back into the depths of the atmos-
phere. The sound of hail and rain,
crashing on the metal roofs, reached
our ears; the last golden dome stood
yet moment in the sunshine, and
then everything swam in the chaos of
dust and storm. So veil by veil fell
over the magical scene, and as the
whirlwind reached us, a void, black
and impenetrable, hid it from our
eyes. We had again witnessed the
destruction of Moscow.

COMMODORE PERRY—The members of the Monizuma Society in this city held special meeting at the Everett House the 9th inst. Capt. Henry Eagle, U. S. N., presided, Capt. J. L. Lowell Secretary of Society. The following preamble and resolutions were duly reported and unanimously adopted:

whereas we have heard with profound regret of the death of Commodore Matthew Perry, United States Navy, late President of this society, be it, therefore,

Resolved, That by his death the navy of the United States only loses of its brightest ornaments but the country at large deprived of the services of an officer who in peace contributed largely to its reputation and influence, and in to its honor and power.

That members of the society which he presided with such kindly courtesy and social urbanity deeply lament the loss of one whose standing and ability placed him high in the list of the honored defenders of his country and whose many noble and generous qualities as a gentleman endeared him to all those who like ourselves enjoyed the pleasure of his personal intercourse.

That we respectfully tender to the family of the deceased deep sympathy in their bereavement with the thought that they are not alone in their sorrow, the memory of Commodore Perry enshrined in the hearts of a legion of warm friends, who respected him as an officer and loved him as a friend.

ST. PATRICK'S DAY—The rival conventions of Irish societies who propose to celebrate St. Patrick's Day have not yet to understanding and it is than likely that there will be none, and that there will be two small celebrations instead of one large one. The organization which Tammany Hall met last night, James Keelan the chair and Thomas Kiven Secretary. After debate, Thomas Herman, of the Quarrymens Union Protective Society chosen Grand Marshal of the procession with power to appoint his aids Messrs. McBride, Tracy and McKennswere appointed committee to confer with the military the route of the procession. It was stated by the Chairman that every effort had been used to induce the Prince street organization to compromise so as to have only one turnout but far all their efforts had been unavailing. They were still however, ready to agree upon any reasonable compromise. The following are the of the societies interested in the Tammany organization, viz. The Ancient Sons of St. Patrick, the Ancient Order of Hibernians, Quarry Union Protective Society; the Workingmens Union Benevolent Society; the Flushing Hibernians, the Hibernian Society, and Green's the Friendly Sons of Erin, the Irish National Guards, the Farrell Guards. The Convention adjourned to again this week when it is hoped that the other organization will come to terms.

The NEW ROOMS FOR THE SUPERVISORS AND COUNCILMEN—The old chamber of the Board of Councilmen has been made into two apartments for the accommodation of the Supervisors and the Board of Councilmen which is a much smaller body than the Board of last year. The room for the Councilmen in readiness for occupancy yesterday, but that for the Supervisors will not be ready before next week. The work commenced at the beginning of the year and had not been a Corporation job would have been finished in a month at first, but city contractors take their time and make up the difference in their bid. The rooms will look very fine; portraits of Jackson, Hull, Henry Clay and Governor Fish will adorn the walls of the Councilmens chamber and both rooms will be pretty and comfortable.

THE LATE MYSTERIOUS DEATH OF YOUNG LADY.—There appears to be a great deal of excitement manifested in Poughkeepsie regarding the sudden and mysterious death of a young lady from that place, an account of which gave in Saturday's Herald. Yesterday morning policeman Brevoor, Deputy superintendent Talmadge, special aid received a letter from Coroner Taylor of Poughkeepsie regarding the matter stating that the friends of the deceased made an animation of the body, and desiring to cooperate with the authorities in this city in investigating the affair, to take the case in hand and proceed to Poughkeepsie immediately and with the assistance of Coroner Taylor have the body exhumed and examined. This will, no doubt, be done on Wednesday.

ANOTHER FERRY TO STATEN ISLAND.—The Committee on Ferries of the Board of Aldermen yesterday in reaction to the petition of several parties residing on Staten Island who desire a slip in this city where they might land their boats from their ferry line from here to Staten Island. Mr. Townsend appeared before the committee and said that the Islanders wish to run a boat from Clifton which is 900 feet below Vanderbilts landing to some part of New York. He built the dock which cost him himself, and cost him $4,600. His object in running the ferry was not to make money out of it but to accommodate the people residing on Staten Island. Alderman Adams said that the best way the committee could manage in the matter is to put the temporary slip to which the New Brighton boats land at auction, and Mr. Townsend would then have opportunity of purchasing the slip for any purpose. Mr. Townsend said he was satisfied to have the slip put up at auction, and added if they got the slip he would ferry every hour to Staten Island. The committee then adjourned.

CORONER CONNERY is rumored yesterday about the CITY Hall that Coroner Connery had been brought before Mayor Tiemann on a charge of neglect of duty on complaint of certain parties living at No. 50 Suffolk street; Mr. Connery, said he had sent his son Edward, youth about sixteen years old, to hold an inquest at the above noted place instead of performing the task himself. The son, alleged, actually held the inquest. The result of Mr. Connery's interview with the Mayor has been made public.

CLOSE OF THE EVENING SCHOOLS—The evening schools throughout the city were formally closed last Friday evening for the season, and the occasion was signaled by appropriate exercises in each of them. This year these schools have been very successful and the attendance has been unusually large. Thousands of poor young men and women have been grateful for the benefit they have received from these institutions and the feeling is general that the educational wants of this class will require evening schools to be kept open during the year, with the exception of perhaps a month in summertime. There is no good reason why the ignorant should have the schools and teachers both unemployed. Let us have evening schools all the year around, gentlemen of the Board of Education.

The story was told by an old man and valued friend now residing in the country near Dayton, Ohio, but whose early days were spent near the tragic adventure here told. We give the story as related in the words of the hero—

It was about the year 1805, that I settled in Virginia, near the falls of Kanawha. The country, at that time, was an unbroken wilderness. But few settlements had been made by the whites, and they were so far apart as to render vain all hopes of assistance in case of any attack from the hostile Indians, numbers of whom still infested the neighborhood.

I lived there alone with my wife for several months, unmolested and by dint of perseverance, being then young and hardy, had succeeded in making quite large clearing in the forest, which I had planted with corn, and which promised an abundant yield.

One morning, after we had dispatched our humble meal, and had just prepared to venture forth upon my regular routine of labor, my attention was arrested by the tinkling of the cowbell in the corn field.

"There," said my wife, "the cow is in the cornfield."

But the ear of the backwoodsman becomes, by nature, very acute, especially so, that his safety often depends upon the cultivation of that sense. I was not so easily deceived. I listened—the sound was repeated.

"That," said I to my wife, "was not the tinkle of a bell upon the neck of a cow. It is a decoy from some Indians, who wish to draw me into ambush."

Believing this to be the case, I took down my old musket, and seeing that it was properly loaded, stole cautiously round the field to the point from which the sound seemed to proceed. As I suspected, there, in a cluster of bushes, crouched an Indian, waiting for me to appear to answer his decoy bell, that he might send a fatal ball to my heart. I approached, without discovering myself to him, until within good shooting distance, then rammed my piece and fired, and the Indian fell dead.

Fearing that he might be accompanied by others, I returned with all speed to the cabin, and having firmly barricaded the door, I watched all day at the portholes, in anticipation of an attack from the companions of the Indian I had killed. To add to the seeming terrors of my situation, I discovered that I had but one charge of powder left. I could make but one shot, and if attacked by numbers, I should be cut off in their power. Determined to do the best with what I had, I poured out the last charge of powder and put it into my musket, and then waited for the approach of night, feeling confident of an attack.

Night came at last—a beautiful moonlight night, too. This favored me greatly, as I would thereby be able to observe the movements of the enemy as they approached my cabin. It was some two hours after nightfall, and yet I had neither heard or seen any signs of Indians, when suddenly I was startled by the baying of my dog at the stable.

The stable and between the two was a patch of ground upon which the light of the full moon fell unobstructed. Judging from the noise at the stable, that they would advance from that direction, I posted myself at the porthole on that side of the cabin.

I had previously placed my wife on the crosspole in the chimney and in case our enemies effected an entrance in the cabin, she might climb out through the low chimney, and effect an escape. For myself I entertained no hope; but determined not to be taken alive, I resolved to sell my life dearly.

With breathless anxiety, I watched at the porthole. At length I saw them emerge from the shadow of the stable, and advance across the vacant ground toward my cabin. One—two—three—four—five—six—Heaven sir! six stalwart Indians armed to the teeth, and urged on by the hope of revenge, and alone to oppose them, with one charge of powder—my case was desperate, indeed.

With quick yet stealthy step, in close single file they approached, and were already within a few yards of the house when a slight change in the movement of the forward Indian, changed the position of the entire six, so that a portion of the left side of each was uncovered.

They were all in range—one aim would have covered all. Quick as thought I aimed and fired.

Saint, by the Rev. F. P. Boyle. The Oliver Hibern-
ian Free School will have its usual celebration
and the children receive their usual annual pres-
ents at 10 o'clock in the morning at the school-
room on North street. In the evening the Hibern-
ian Society and Emmett Club will partake of their
usual anniversary feast.


BURGLARY AND ARRESTS.—Yesterday morning
about 8 o'clock the boot and shoe store of Mrs. Car-
oline Harrod, a widow, was entered by thieves and
property to the amount of about $50 was carried
away. The robbers obtained an entrance by forcing
open the back door of the building with a hose
wrench, which was found on the premises. Upon
the discovery of the burglary word sent to the T.
u. Police Station, when Lieut. Muir, with officers
Baylor and Denham were detailed to make arrests
of the guilty parties. Suspicious circumstances
drew the attention of the officers to two men, named
John McGinn and John Alterhoff, whereupon they
were both arrested and taken to the station house.
McGinn had on his feet a pair of new boots, which
were readily recognized by Mrs. Harrod. Upon an
examination before Justice Audoun, Alterhoff was
discharged, there being no evidence against him to
connect him with the robbery. McGinn was sent
to jail to stand trial before the Criminal
Court.


Subsequently, a man by the name of Aaron Back-
crack, who keeps a second hand shop on Canton
Avenue near Caroline street, was arrested by Ser-
geant Smith, on the charge of having received the
above goods, knowing them to be stolen. He was
taken before Justice Audoun, who released him on
$500 security for a further examination which will
take place this afternoon.


HIGHWAY ROBBERY.—On Monday night about 10
o'clock a gentleman, accompanied by his wife,
was returning home from a place of amusement,
and while passing along Centre Market space, they
were met by three ruffians, who unceremoniously
jostled against them; at the same time one of them
suddenly jerked the gentleman's watch and chain
from his vest when the three made tracks to parts
unknown.


SERIOUS CASUALTY.—Mr. Jacob Hays, a ship car-
penter, yesterday morning met with an accident at
his residence on Light street extended, by falling
down a flight of stairs. His left leg was broken
above the knee, besides which he sustained injuries
upon the body of a serious nature. Dr. Baltzell
was called in who set the limb and dressed the in-
juries.


CHARGE OF PASSING COUNTERFEIT MONEY.—Edward
I. Ards was arrested yesterday by officers Bishop
and Elderkin, of the Western District police, on
the charge OF attempting to pass a counterfeit five
dollar note, purporting to be of the City Bank of
New Haven, Conn, upon Mr. John Gusts, lottery
dealer, on W. Baltimore street. He was committed
to answer by Justice Logan.


ARREST For STEALING.—Charles Wallis (colored)
was taken into custody yesterday by officer Van
Saint, of the Southern District Police on the charge
Of stealing from his employer, William Thomas,
also colored, the sum of $11. He was committed
BY Justice Spies to await an examination.


IMPROVING.—The daughter of Mr. James Hughes
who was seriously injured the 9th inst. by being
caught in some of the machinery of the spice mills
near the corner of Caroline and Fayette streets is
slowly improving under the careful attention of Dr.
Clendinen.

train to Washington.

WHEREAS, the last General Assembly of South
Carolina, with a wise forecast, and a liberal regard for the public welfare, based essentially
on the good sense and virtue of her citizens enacted
law by which the Commissioners of Free Schools are
authorized to establish Normal School in the city of
Charleston to which the country districts will be entitled to send certain number of pupils.

And whereas the enterprising Board of St. Philip's
and St. Michael's have now in operation, at their present public school in the city, weekly exercises,
which will serve to exemplify the benefits of such an
establishment.

Now, Therefore, recommend to the several Boards
of Commissioners of Free Schools in the State to appoint at their next quarterly meeting on the fourth
Monday in April and depute one or more of their
number to visit the said public school St. Philip's
street, in Charleston at their convenience so as to be
able to report the result of their observations at the
quarterly meeting, on the fourth Monday of October
next.

Also, do hereby invite all the Teachers of Free
Schools and scholars throughout the State to come and see
for themselves how the said Public School is conducted
and what are the uses of a Normal School.

As the expenses of such visit might put it out of
the power of many to come, however much they may
desire it, we will venture to say for the good citizens of
Charleston that the houses of many residents will be
opened to any Teacher who shall be provided with a
letter of introduction or with the certificates of the President and Secretary of the Board of Commissioners.
In this or in case public house
is preferred, affords me pleasure to announce that
Mrs. Kennedy, of the American Hotel, in King street
on account of this Department, will take care of any
Teacher of Free School who will deposit with her
his or her certificates from the President and Secretary of the District Board of Commissioners on or which
he or she may be employed from the first of June to
the fifth inclusive.

Furthermore, appeal to the proper authorities of
the railroads and other public conveyances by means
of which they must reach the city, to instruct their
several agents, upon the exhibition to them of the said
certificates to pass all such Teachers of Free Schools
and one Commissioner from each Board going down
for the purpose herein set forth for one going
and returning.

I am assured that the Commissioners of Free Schools
of St. Philip's and St. Michael's will take pleasure in
affording every facility to the Teachers and others to
observe and profit by the improved methods. Those
only having to apply to E. G. MEMMINGER, ESQ.,
Chairman, or to any member of the Board, at the
Public School House, in St. Philip's street, to be admitted at the proper hours.

A fixed time has been mentioned from the first to
the fifth of June. It is better for all parties to adopt this appointment; but if there
be impediments to prevent any Teachers from coming
at that time, the Commissioners will receive them at
any other time in May or June, including Saturdays
of the days.

Given under my hand and the seal of the State at
Chicora, near Georgetown, this second day of April
in the year of our Lord one thousand eight
hundred and fifty-eight, and in the eighty-second year
of our Independence.

RUBY F. FELSENGER,
W. R. LUDWIG, Deputy Secretary of State.

April 2nd, 1858.

MURDER AT MARIPOSA.--On Sunday last at
about 10 o'clock A.M. some of our citizens near
the corner of Main and Fifth streets were alarm
ed by the report of pistol in the direction of
the Chinese houses in that neighborhood. Sev
eral persons proceeded in the direction of the
shooting and upon arriving at the yard, ad-
joining, found a man by the name of Francis
Kerrins lying in the agonies of death, the blood
gushing from his mouth and nostrils. It was
supposed that he was shot at or about the spot
where he was found, which was about twenty
yards from the house, as he was seen on the
street few minutes before. The buildings
were surrounded and search made for the mur-
derer. A Chinaman was seen with pistol in
his hand by some of those who first arrived on
the ground, but could not be identified. No
pistol could be found about the place. Several
arrests were made, and strict investigation
will be made with view of detecting the au-
thor of this crime.

burn, Esq, summoned jury of inquest who,

The BRIGHT, ENGLISH AND FOLEY
PURCHASE.—The gentleman who made
the first disclosures of Bright, English
and Foley's land operations, with the Q.
L. Land Office Commissioner, has deemed
it proper to give all the particulars OF
the transaction, in letter to General
Spinner, a member of Congress from
New York, who first called the attention
of Congress to the matter. The follow-
ing is his communication.

DEAR Sir: I notice that you have recent-

ly called the attention of the House and
the country to the circumstances attending
the purchase of a large body of land by the
Hon. Jesse D. Bright and others at the Land
Office in this city, as detailed in letter
published in The Burlington Hawkeye, and
written by himself. From the proceedings
of the House, I think the facts were not
clearly understood, and the real point of
complaint in the matter was passed over un-
noticed. I desire, therefore, to detail the
facts to you as they occurred, as I have learn-
ed them from the Registers and Receiver's
offices at this place, and as they were an-
nounced at the time of the occurrences.
It should be understood, at the outset,
that for four weeks after the Land Office in
this city was opened for private entry on th'
23rd of February, the number of persons de-
siring to enter lands was so great that the
Register adopted a rule requiring every per-
son wishing to enter land to enter his name
on a register kept for the purpose, and each
name was then called in its regular turn of
order, and each person was allowed to enter
one section, or 640 acres of land only, when
his name was thus reached. If the appli-
cant desired more land, he put his name at
the foot of the register, and then waited
to be reached again. This rule worked hard
upon those desiring to enter large quan-
tities of land, but, as it served all alike, all cheer-
fully acquiesced in its continuance.

The regular hours of opening the office
of the Register, in which the entries were
made, was 9 o'clock in the morning; but on
the morning of the 11th of March, the doc-
tors were kept closed for nearly an hour after
the time, although the crowd of applicants in at-
tendance was as large as ever, and all were
surprised, and some indignant, that the con-
tinuance of the day's work should be so
long delayed. But finally the doors were
opened and the crowd admitted, and we were
then told by the clerks that they had been
busily engaged all the morning in enter-
ing 5000 acres of land for the Hon. Jesse
Bright, by special order of the Commiss'o-
ner of the General Land Office, received the
previous evening.

On further inquiry, it appears that
the orders of the Commissioner were to en-
ter the land for Mr. Bright and Messrs. Engli-
sh and Foley immediately on the receipt of
order, and the Register therefore felt him-
self compelled to override the rule he had made,
and enter the lands in the manner he had
stated, with the doors locked, and without
giving others an opportunity to offer com-
peting applications.

The amount thus entered was:

On Saturday morning little fellow, about eight years
old, of Mr. Gilleau, bookseller, while playing
with some other boys on North street, approached a

gray frosted surface, when, in an instant, to the
boy's own horror and utter astonishment of his
playmates, he was held fast by his tongue to the
post suffering very severe pain, and totally unable
to help or extricate himself. Of course the boy
could not speak, and could only manifest his feel
ings by signs with his hands. Various applications
of warm tea, steam, etc. were made by some neigh
bors who heard the usual noise made by the other
boys, and came to learn what was the matter, but
of no avail; such was the action of the cold iron that
the hold was even getting tighter. When after ten
minutes had elapsed, the boy's father heard of the
affair, and fastening to his relief, he took knife
and was obliged to cut the tongue loose, leaving its
skin still fast to the post and causing the blood to
flow very profusely. Immediately on his release,
the poor little fellow became insensible, and was
taken home. — London &c. W. Press, Nov. p.

NEW YORK, June -
Patrick Slane's glass factory at Williamsburg was
demolished yesterday afternoon by the storm.
There were thirty persons in the building at the
time all of whom were buried in the ruins, but only
two were killed and six or eight wounded. The
killed are Bernard Slane, father of the proprietor,
and Thomas Gill, the engineer. Mr. Slane's loss is
$4,000.


Rev. Ralph Hoyt's new Church in this city was
entirely demolished. Loss $4,000.


Much other damage was done to buildings in the
city and vicinity and to the shipping in the harbor.
Many persons were more or less injured.


The lightning struck in some dozen places, but
the only death reported from this cause is that of
BRIDGET Farrell, of Brooklyn, who had rushed into
the street to recover her child from the storm,
when she was instantly struck down.

of Mrs. Brennan, wife of Capt. Brennan, of the U. S.
army, who, it will be remembered left Staten Island on

heard from since.

Dr. Crane, the brother of the lady gave the police the

possively questioned on the subject and one of them

are satisfied that she was robbed or worse treated,
murdered and thrown into the middle of the river.
